purpose: The in-package digest mismatches that ALREADY EXIST in the committed tree. Recorded as data rather than excluded in code, so the guard fails on a NEW one without failing forever on an old one that cannot be corrected without rewriting an accepted package.
howEachWasEstablished: For every entry the working tree byte-for-byte equals HEAD, and neither equals the digest the same commit recorded. So the disagreement was baked in when the package was committed; nothing in the working tree mutated it, and §263 did not cause it.
notARepair: §263 does NOT rewrite these manifests or these members. Correcting a frozen manifest to agree with the bytes it failed to describe would destroy the only record that they ever disagreed.

The tracked file is absent, and an untracked file in the same directory, 'ecfr-1910-146 4.xml', is byte-identical to the deleted file in HEAD -- both digest to d3dc555e5e783af729b8243ba7932aff... A sibling 'ecfr-1910-146 2.xml' is also present. This is a filename duplication performed outside git, not a deletion of regulatory source evidence.
preExistingWorktreeState.predates: §262 and §263; it was present in the working tree before either section began
preExistingWorktreeState.sectionAction: §263 does NOT rename, restore or delete it. It is unrelated worktree content, and correcting it is a deliberate act for the product owner: `git mv 'ecfr-1910-146 4.xml' ecfr-1910-146.xml` after confirming which duplicate is wanted.
preExistingWorktreeState.guardTreatment: Reported on every run as PRE-EXISTING and excluded from the exit code, so the guard fails on drift introduced by the CURRENT session rather than failing forever on a condition it is not authorized to fix.

externalReferenceDriftIsNotAFault: 66 manifest lines name files OUTSIDE their package -- live source under backend/, documents under docs/. Their digests record what those files were when the section froze. The files have legitimately moved on. Treating that as corruption would mean every future source edit corrupts the evidence base.
